newsitem.title: USA: Clinton, Republicans announce landmark budget deal.
newsitem.headline: Clinton, Republicans announce landmark budget deal.

text.p: President Bill Clinton announced on Friday that he had reached a landmark agreement with Republican leaders in Congress on a plan to balance the federal budget by 2002.
"We have reached agreement in broad but fairly specific terms ... with Republican leaders today that would balance the budget by 2002," Clinton announced during a trip to Baltimore.

The outline plan, also announced by Republican leaders at the Capitol in Washington, has already been attacked by some Democrats and Republicans and is expected to be the subject of intense negotiation in coming months.

If the plan is passed by the Republican-held Congress and the economy performs as forecast, 2002 would mark the first time the federal government's accounts were in balance since 1969, when President Richard Nixon was in office.
"We have a deal, now comes the hard part -- selling it to Congress," said one official who accompanied Clinton to Baltimore, Maryland, where he was meeting Senate Democrats at a retreat.
Senate Democratic leader Tom Daschle, accompanying Clinton, told reporters: "I am confident today that the majority of Democrats in the United States Senate will support this agreement."

Documents detailing the pact, given to reporters in Washington, said it would slow growth in spending on the Medicare health programme for the elderly by $115 billion over five years and offer a net $85 billion in tax cuts including a reduction in the capital gains tax on investments, a child tax credit, and some relief from inheritance taxes.
One of the chief Republican negotiators, Sen. Pete Domenici of New Mexico, quickly blessed the pact, saying: "I'm very happy with the agreement."

A deal would mark a stunning breakthrough on an issue that has snarled U.S. politics for years and one that would enable both Democrat Clinton and the Republican-held Congress to claim victory over one of America's most intractable problems.
The Democratic White House and Republican Congress have been at loggerheads over the budget since Republicans won majority control of both U.S. legislative chambers in 1994.
The two sides failed to reach a balanced budget agreement over the ensuing two years, leading to two partial shut-downs of the federal government in late 1995 and early 1996.
